You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's principal shapes and meaningful internal boundaries represented with pencil-like contour linework?
node.criteria: Pass if convincing drawn, sketch-like contours describe the principal forms and meaningful internal boundaries across the scene, with pencil-like stroke articulation or variable line weight. Coverage must be broadly present, but every object and boundary need not be perfectly drawn. Fail if the principal contours remain photographic or merely show stronger edges or sharpening halos without convincing drawn linework. Desaturation and uniform grain alone do not satisfy this condition. Judge contours independently of interior shading. Use unknown only when the visual evidence is insufficient to establish the contour style.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the requested pencil-drawing transformation. Inspect contours of the plate, food, fork, glass and pitcher, distinguishing added pencil-like linework from photographic edges already present in the source. The target is pencil-drawn representation of the image's visual content; the reference is the supplied image and requested pencil-drawing transformation.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image is desaturated and grainy, but the plate, food, fork, glass, and pitcher mostly retain soft photographic edges. There is no convincing, broadly present pencil-like contour linework or clear stroke articulation; the visible texture alone does not establish drawn contours.

d1_shading: The trace identifies real progress—desaturation, grain, and stronger outlines—but judges only the shading criterion, so its `fail` should not be treated as evidence that no requested change occurred. Keep this node narrowly focused on whether tonal rendering is pencil-like, and preserve the distinction between partial stylistic progress and full fulfillment for the aggregate rubric. The edited image has visibly altered, muted, grainy surfaces, yet the pitcher and glass retain smooth reflective gradients and much of the food retains photographic-looking texture; assess those observations against the stated shading criteria rather than equating grain or desaturation with graphite shading. The binding already names the relevant regions, so clarify that the comparison should inspect both the character and extent of graphite-like tonal marks across them, while allowing smooth or rubbed graphite where convincing and avoiding a fail based on isolated imperfect surfaces. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is reported; the disagreement is semantic/criterion calibration, not missing execution.

response.content: {"text":"The node is already narrowly scoped to contours, and its trace is valid with no transport, schema, or dependency failure. Improve the binding so the decision explicitly compares the edited image with the source and judges whether the requested transformation has made meaningful progress toward pencil-like contours—not only whether contours fully pass the completion criterion. The edit visibly changes color and texture, but the trace reports that principal edges remain mostly photographic; keep that negative contour evidence distinct from the separate evidence of stylistic progress, so a contour-level fail does not imply that the overall request made no progress. Preserve the criterion that contours must be convincingly drawn and broadly present; do not count desaturation, grain, or stronger photographic edges as contour fulfillment. Ask for evidence tied to the named forms and their internal boundaries, and reserve unknown for genuinely insufficient visual evidence rather than using it to soften a clear negative finding.
